tagline.text: The best white-water rafting river in northern Luzon, running through the Kalinga valleys

location.label: Location
location.text: Mountain Province to Kalinga (rafting base is Tabuk City, Kalinga)

children.text: The Chico River is a major river of northern Luzon that flows from Mountain Province through Kalinga to the Cagayan River, and Class III–IV white-water rafting runs operate from Tabuk City in Kalinga. It is also famous for the Kalinga people's resistance to a dam plan in the 1970s.

The Chico River begins in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon and flows through Mountain Province, Kalinga and Cagayan to join the Cagayan River. Wikipedia gives its length as about 233 km and calls it the longest tributary of the Cagayan River, but some travel guides put it at around 170 km, so figures differ by source. The farthest headwaters rise on the slopes of Mount Data in Bauko, Mountain Province, and it meets the Cagayan River at Santo Niño, Cagayan. It passes towns such as Bontoc, Sabangan, Sadanga, Tinglayan, Lubuagan, Tabuk and Pinukpuk. The basin covers about 5,850 sq km and the average discharge is said to be about 410 cubic meters per second, with tributaries such as the Pasil, Saltan and Mabaca joining from the left and the Bunog, Tanudan and Biga from the right. Because it flows at higher elevation, it is also said to flood less than the Cagayan River.

For travelers, the Chico River is best known for white-water rafting. The base is Tabuk City, the capital of Kalinga, and the main runs are the Mataguan Run from Tinglayan to Pasil and the Ullalim Run from Pasil to Tabuk. The middle of the scale is Class III–IV on the international scale, and in the rainy season it is said to reach Class V. According to one news report, the main operator runs only about two trips a month even during the rafting season, so book ahead. A 2002 Philippine Star article described seven rapids on the roughly 20 km stretch from Pasil, and said the strongest, once nicknamed God's Playground, had disappeared. Rapids change from year to year, so ask your operator about current conditions.

The Kalinga people call this river a river of life, because farming, trade, laundry and bathing carabao are all tied to it. When the Marcos government planned four hydroelectric dams on the Chico in the 1970s, the Kalinga and Bontoc peoples joined in opposing it through a peace pact called a bodong. Macli-ing Dulag, a leader of that resistance, was killed in 1980, and the plan was dropped in the 1980s. April 24 is now observed as Cordillera Day. A United Nations special rapporteur estimated that about 300,000 people would have been affected by the dam plan. For this reason the Chico River is often cited in the Philippines as a case study on ancestral domain.

Tabuk City is a quiet highland city with no shopping malls or busy nightlife, about 480 km from Manila. Beyond rafting there are sights scattered around, such as the traditional tattooing of Buscalan, rice terraces, waterfalls and hot springs, so many trips are built around rafting and a long loop through northern Cordillera.

This run is recommended for beginners. You travel about 20 km from the Pasil tributary to Tabuk, mostly through Class III rapids. One guide lists a one-day package at about ₱4,000 per person (including hotel, breakfast, equipment and transport, an old rate). The road from Pasil to Tabuk is rough, and the drive takes about an hour and a half.

An advanced run through rice terraces and limestone canyons, with Class III–V rapids one after another. According to the guide, it is a two-day trip with lodging, and an old rate of about ₱7,000 per person is listed. If you have no experience, always talk to the operator first.

blocks.title: A rafting trip starting from Tabuk

children.text: The usual plan is to stay a night in a hotel in Tabuk and go rafting the next day. The operator provides a helmet and life vest, and explains how to read the water and what to do if you fall out of the boat.

blocks.title: The river of the Kalinga people

children.text: Villagers along the river depend on it for daily life, including farming, bathing and feeding carabao. From a boat you can see the river up close as it flows between rice fields and villages.

Bugnay, near Tinglayan in the upper river, is the hometown of Macli-ing Dulag. Knowing the history of how the Kalinga and Bontoc peoples joined forces to stop the dam plan makes the river look different. Macli-ing Dulag was born in Bugnay in 1930, served three terms as barrio captain, and in 1974 convened a bodong, a peace council, in Tanglag. In May 1975 a bodong of about 150 Bontoc and Kalinga leaders produced the Pagta ti Bodong pact.

Some tour itineraries raft the upper stretch from Bontoc to Anabel and then move on to Tinglayan. It is described as having consecutive Class III rapids and several Class IV. The six-day itinerary of Uncharted Philippines goes from Manila to Banaue, Bontoc, Maligcong and Buscalan and Tulgao in Tinglayan, then rafts the lower river from Tabuk and returns to Manila. It is a private tour for four or more at about US$1,060 per person, and moderate fitness for 2–4 hours of walking a day is said to be needed.

Around Tabuk, sights include St. William's Cathedral, the rice terraces of Tinglayan, Matabor Falls, Palan-ah Falls, Pasil Dam and the Kalinga hot springs. It is worth staying a day longer before or after rafting. Older guides also mention destinations such as Balbalasang-Balbalan National Park, the Uguid-Maling underground river, Aguinaldo Hill and the Buaya caves. Check each location and whether it is open locally first.

Chico River rafting runs in the rainy season, when the water rises. The Inquirer says August to December is peak rafting season, and other sources say trips run from June to December. In the rainy season the water level is said to rise to Class V, so beginners must talk to an operator beforehand.

In the dry season (November–May), by contrast, stretches of the river are low and rafting can be difficult. This is, however, a good time to explore the Kalinga mountain roads and the nearby waterfalls and rice terraces.

Tabuk has no malls or busy nightlife, but it has several simple hotels and lodges. Older sources list Davidson Hotel, Bilza Lodge, Kalinga Hostel, Mahogany Lodge and others, but whether they still operate and at what rates needs to be checked. Rafting packages usually include one hotel night, breakfast, equipment and transport.
For meals, people generally use restaurants in Tabuk and hotel restaurants. Kalinga is mountainous, so confirm lodging and restaurants in advance and bring plenty of cash.

If you are traveling a long way, it is safer to spend the last night in Tabuk. In the rainy season the water rises so far that reports describe floods reaching villages 20 m above the bank, so if heavy rain fell the day before your rafting, follow the operator's judgment. On days you travel from Tabuk toward Tinglayan or Bontoc, the mountain roads are long, so set out early in the morning.
The operator provides a helmet and life vest and gives a safety briefing, and you must follow it.
If you cannot swim or have never done Class III or above, start with the Ullalim Run.
Bring a waterproof bag, spare clothes and sandals or shoes that can get wet.
Rain can change your plans in the rainy season, so leave at least one spare day.
Operators may form teams only a few times a month, so book weeks ahead.
On the way from Tabuk toward Bontoc and Sagada, you can add Tinglayan and Buscalan.
Bring plenty of cash. ATMs are hard to find in the mountain areas.
Check the Manila–Tuguegarao flight route first. Domestic flight schedules change by season.
In the rainy season the river can reach Class V and floods sometimes inundate villages, so always go with an experienced operator.
Many of the prices and contact numbers come from sources dated around 2012–2018 and may differ from today. Confirm before booking.
Falling out of the boat is common in white-water rafting. Wear your helmet and life vest at all times.
Mountain roads are dusty and narrow, and landslides can occur in the rainy season, so avoid night travel.
The riverbank is where villagers live and work. Ask permission before photographing people who are bathing or washing.
A 2014 report said quarrying on the Kalinga river was banned. Help protect the environment and do not leave any trash.
